summary.text: Assuming either family is finite, bound it by \(B\) and apply positivity at \(n=(B+7)!/6\) to obtain primes \(p=6x-1\) and \(q=6y+1\) with \(p+q=(B+7)!\), where \(p\) is Sophie Germain and \(q-2,q\) are twins. The relevant bound makes either \(p\), or in the twin case \(q\), divide the factorial and hence the complementary prime; primality would force equality (apart from the impossible divisor \(1\)), contradicting \(p\equiv-1\pmod 6\) and \(q\equiv1\pmod 6\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
\mathcal S=\{p\in\mathbb N: p\text{ is prime and }2p+1\text{ is prime}\}
\]
be the set of Sophie Germain primes, and let
\[
\mathcal T=\{p\in\mathbb N: p\text{ is prime and }p+2\text{ is prime}\}
\]
be the set of smaller members of twin-prime pairs.

For a positive integer \(n\), the quantity \(a(n)=A227923(n)\) counts those integers \(x\) with \(1\le x<n\) for which, on putting \(y=n-x\), all four numbers
\[
6x-1,\qquad 12x-1,\qquad 6y-1,\qquad 6y+1
\]
are prime. Thus \(6x-1\) is a Sophie Germain prime, because
\[
2(6x-1)+1=12x-1,
\]
and \(6y-1,6y+1\) form a twin-prime pair.

Assume throughout that
\[
a(n)>0\qquad\text{for every integer }n>1.
\]
We prove that both \(\mathcal S\) and \(\mathcal T\) are infinite.

First we establish the common extraction step used in both arguments. Fix any integer \(M\ge 7\), and set
\[
n=\frac{M!}{6}.
\]
Since \(6\le M\), the number \(6\) divides \(M!\), so this quotient is an integer and
\[
6n=M!.
\]
Moreover, factorials are increasing from this point onward, so
\[
M!\ge 7!=5040,
\]
and hence
\[
n=\frac{M!}{6}\ge 840>1.
\]
By the hypothesis, \(a(n)>0\). Since \(a(n)\) is a sum of terms each equal to either \(0\) or \(1\), at least one term in that sum equals \(1\). Consequently, there is an integer \(x\) with
\[
1\le x<n
\]
such that, upon defining \(y=n-x\), the four numbers
\[
6x-1,\quad 12x-1,\quad 6y-1,\quad 6y+1
\]
are all prime. The inequality \(x<n\) implies \(y=n-x\ge1\). Also \(x+y=n\), and therefore
\[
(6x-1)+(6y+1)=6(x+y)=6n=M!.
\]
Thus, for every \(M\ge7\), we can find positive integers \(x,y\) such that
\[
6x-1,\ 12x-1,\ 6y-1,\ 6y+1
\]
are all prime and
\[
(6x-1)+(6y+1)=M!. \tag{1}
\]

We now prove that there are infinitely many Sophie Germain primes. Suppose, for contradiction, that \(\mathcal S\) is finite. Every finite set of natural numbers has an upper bound, so choose \(B\in\mathbb N\) such that
\[
p\le B\qquad\text{for every }p\in\mathcal S.
\]
Apply the extraction step with
\[
M=B+7,
\]
which is at least \(7\). We obtain positive integers \(x,y\) satisfying the primality conditions above and
\[
(6x-1)+(6y+1)=(B+7)!. \tag{2}
\]
Put
\[
p=6x-1,\qquad q=6y+1.
\]
The number \(p\) is in \(\mathcal S\): it is prime, and
\[
2p+1=2(6x-1)+1=12x-1
\]
is prime. Hence the choice of \(B\) gives \(p\le B\). Also \(x\ge1\), so \(p=6x-1\ge5\), in particular \(1\le p\le B+7\). Every positive integer at most \(B+7\) divides \((B+7)!\), and therefore
\[
p\mid (B+7)!.
\]
Equation (2) says \((B+7)!=p+q\). Since \(p\) divides both \((B+7)!\) and \(p\), it follows that \(p\mid q\).

But \(q=6y+1\) is prime. A positive divisor of a prime is either \(1\) or the prime itself, so either
\[
p=1
\]
or
\[
p=q.
\]
The first possibility is impossible because \(p\ge5\). The second is also impossible: \(p=6x-1\) is congruent to \(5\pmod 6\), whereas \(q=6y+1\) is congruent to \(1\pmod 6\). Equivalently, equality would give
\[
6x-1=6y+1,
\]
and hence \(6(x-y)=2\), which is impossible. This contradiction shows that \(\mathcal S\) is infinite.

It remains to prove that there are infinitely many twin-prime pairs. Suppose, again for contradiction, that \(\mathcal T\) is finite. Choose an upper bound \(B\in\mathbb N\) for it, so that
\[
r\le B\qquad\text{for every }r\in\mathcal T.
\]
Apply the extraction step with \(M=B+7\). This gives positive integers \(x,y\) for which all four relevant numbers are prime and
\[
(6x-1)+(6y+1)=(B+7)!. \tag{3}
\]
Set
\[
r=6y-1,\qquad q=6y+1=r+2,
\]
and also set
\[
p=6x-1.
\]
Both \(r\) and \(r+2=q\) are prime, so \(r\in\mathcal T\). Hence \(r\le B\), and consequently
\[
q=r+2\le B+2\le B+7.
\]
Since \(y\ge1\), we also have \(q=6y+1\ge7\). Thus \(q\) is a positive integer no greater than \(B+7\), so
\[
q\mid (B+7)!.
\]
By (3), \((B+7)!=p+q\). Since \(q\) divides both the factorial and itself, it follows that
\[
q\mid p.
\]
The number \(p=6x-1\) is prime. Therefore its positive divisor \(q\) must be either \(1\) or \(p\). It cannot be \(1\), because \(q\ge7\). It also cannot equal \(p\), since
\[
q=6y+1\equiv1\pmod6,
\qquad
p=6x-1\equiv5\pmod6.
\]
This is a contradiction. Hence \(\mathcal T\) is infinite.

We have proved that if \(a(n)>0\) for every integer \(n>1\), then there are infinitely many Sophie Germain primes and infinitely many twin-prime pairs.
